**Recent major news for Bun, the all-in-one JavaScript runtime, bundler, test runner, and package manager, centers on the release of Bun v1.4 in August 2026.**[[1]](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)

### Key Highlights from Bun v1.4 (August 20, 2026)
- **Rewrite from Zig to Rust**: The entire runtime (roughly 780,000–1 million lines of code) was ported to Rust, primarily using AI tools (around 64 parallel Claude agents over 11 days, with over 6,700 commits). The goal was to eliminate entire classes of memory bugs at compile time rather than fixing them individually. This is the first stable release built in Rust; prior versions (up to 1.3.14) used Zig.[[2]](https://appwrite.io/blog/post/announcing-bun-1-4-runtime)
- **Performance and resource improvements**:
  - Idle CPU usage reduced by up to 5x.
  - Memory usage cut by up to 35–48% for HTTP servers (e.g., Fastify from 233 MB to 120 MB peak; Express from 169 MB to 92 MB).
  - Startup 50% faster on Linux (hello-world from ~10.9 ms to 5.1 ms) and ~2.5x faster on Windows.
  - Smaller binary size (up to 17% on Linux/Windows).
  - Production gains observed in large apps like Claude Code (p99 CPU from 24% to 10%).[[3]](https://scrydon.com/insights/2026/08/21/bun-1-4-at-scrydon/)
- **Node.js compatibility**: Passes +1,517 more tests from the Node.js test suite (biggest jump since v1.0). Now reports as Node.js 26 compatible. Many modules (`node:http`, `node:fs`, etc.) pass 97–100% of Node’s own tests. This has enabled better support for tools like Playwright, Next.js 16, Vitest, OpenTelemetry, Nuxt, and others out of the box.[[4]](https://daily.dev/posts/bun-1-4-nz2dmgftt)
- **New built-in APIs and features**:
  - `Bun.Image` (faster image processing than Sharp).
  - `Bun.WebView` (headless browser automation using system WebKit or Chrome via CDP—no extra dependencies like Puppeteer).
  - `Bun.markdown`, `Bun.cron()`, `Bun.Terminal` (PTY support).
  - Native `ReadableStream`/`WritableStream`/`TransformStream`, `CompressionStream`/`DecompressionStream`.
  - ~3x faster `bun:ffi`.
  - Experimental HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 support in `Bun.serve()` and `fetch()`.
  - CLI enhancements: `bun run --parallel`, `bun test --parallel`, `bun audit fix`, `bun dedupe`, `bun prune`, directory serving, Range/conditional requests, and Windows ARM64 support.[[5]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i38DgEuaJwM)

The official release blog, announcement video, and GitHub repo provide full details and upgrade instructions (`bun upgrade`).[[1]](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4)

### Background and Other Recent Developments
- **Acquisition by Anthropic**: In December 2025, Anthropic acquired the Bun project (originally from Oven, founded by Jarred Sumner). It remains fully open-source under the MIT license. The acquisition has accelerated development, with Bun now powering parts of Claude Code and the Claude Agent SDK. Monthly downloads reportedly grew to over 20 million.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bun_(software))
- **Rust rewrite context**: The transition began experimentally in mid-2026 and sparked some community discussion around development practices (heavy AI use, high number of open PRs, and bot-generated commits). However, the v1.4 release emphasizes stability gains, with real-world production metrics from services like Scrydon and Appwrite showing strong improvements. Some developers previously raised concerns about memory leaks and maturity in earlier versions, but v1.4 directly targets these.[[7]](https://daily.dev/posts/bun-1-4-finally-ships-the-rust-rewrite-drama-isn-t-over--fdy7op2yl)
- **Adoption**: Platforms like Appwrite now offer Bun 1.4 as a runtime for Functions and Sites builds. It’s positioned as production-ready for new (“greenfield”) projects, with ongoing canary releases (e.g., 1.4.0-canary builds in early September 2026).[[2]](https://appwrite.io/blog/post/announcing-bun-1-4-runtime)

For the latest, check the official Bun blog (bun.com/blog), GitHub (oven-sh/bun, now at ~96k stars), or their X/Twitter (@bunjavascript). The project continues rapid iteration, with the Rust foundation expected to enable faster future improvements.
